lens: Seriousness and confidence: three sceptical experts (complex systems, process and Chinese philosophy, AI safety), five minutes each, deciding whether this earns an hour
in_one_paragraph: Ren is right about the face, and the cause is specific: the first screen makes the largest possible claim ("how anything forms, lasts, changes and ends") and then, before giving one reason to stay, tells the visitor three times why to leave ("This version is still being revised", "no independent human review is recorded yet", "each central result near-definitional or a known result restated", and a test tally a reader computes as 4 of 36). Two voices sit on the same page and never meet: a prophetic first person ("I take it to be the truth, the dharma, the Dao") and a deflationary audit. In between are counts offered as credentials (532 of 563, 1,183 claims, 3,287 nodes, 1,669 premises), reading times to the minute, board codes and tool paths, and sentences averaging 36 words. All three experts leave, each for a different reason: the scientist at the scope, the philosopher at a "map of wisdom" whose Indigenous and African page says it was written from memory, the safety researcher at a use paragraph that ends "No test designed from it has yet run on a deployed pipeline". Yet the work holds things that would earn an hour, and none is recognisable in two minutes: a machine-checked lock theorem with an experiment that went against the thesis built on it and was kept; a lake experiment in which nothing the fishers were not told of was ever kept; 59 classical Chinese sentences put to a proof checker, some refuted, with the account's own position recorded as the one Nagarjuna refutes; and a prior-art table that names the closest known result for every central law. That last table is the single most confidence-earning object in the repository, and the home page reports only its negative verdict. The fix is not more hedging or less honesty: it is one byline, one claim sized to what is shown, three lead items, the limits said once in two sentences, and everything generated moved behind them.

demonstration:
THE THREE LEAD ITEMS, as they would appear on the first screen (each true to its page).

1. A rule read from its own winners can lock while a loss it does not read grows without bound.
Proved in Lean with no axiom, for a stated model: where a selection's rule, and the way that rule is read, are both formed from the share it selects, a course once locked stays locked however large a loss outside that share becomes; what leaves is a reading of what lies beyond the share. Its nearest known results are lock-in under increasing returns (Arthur 1989) and regulatory capture (Stigler 1971). We tested one reading of it on a language-model judge scoring its own answers, with predictions fixed first: a single note of the loss, from the one disfavoured reader among nine, turned the judge (prose in all 50 picks, against lists in 60 of 60 without the note). That is a case our thesis, as then worded, said would not happen; it is kept as a counterexample for trained judges.
[theorem: records/closed-capture · test: experiments/self-rewarding-lock]

2. What the fishers were not told of, no instruction saved.
Three language-model fishers share a lake (after GovSim). A bed of mussels that gives them nothing dies the first month fewer than 70 tons of fish are left; the community's best steady catch, 50 tons, ends it, and 30 keeps it at 40% of the catch. Told nothing of the bed, they kept it in no season under any instruction, including one to count everything whose continuation depends on their fishing. Told of it and able to talk, one model of two kept it in 8 of 10 seasons with that instruction and 3 of 10 with the community's goal alone; the other model failed three of four predictions, and in the first round, without talk, five of seven failed. Ten seasons a cell, two small models, predictions fixed before any run.

3. Fifty-nine sentences from the Chinese classics, put to a proof checker.
Read as statements about relations, some hold for every relation, some hold only under a premise, and some fail: Mozi's line that two overlapping measures never exhaust each other has a countermodel, and "all things arise from conditions" turns out to be a premise of a model, not a law. Laozi 77's "the way of heaven takes from what has too much" is entered as scope (it is what a two-sided regulation does, not a law of the whole), and its next line, "the human way takes from those who lack", as agreement with a proved law: one member rises only as another falls. The account's own answer on continuity is the position Nagarjuna refutes in the Madhyamaka verses, chapter 21, and that is recorded as open. The readings are ours, made with AI, and wait for scholars of the texts.
[chapter 06 (Chinese) · review/BUDDHIST-THOUGHT B-02 · the drawn bow, USES-EXAMPLES]

THE LIMITS, in two sentences in place of the status paragraph:
This is a formal unification, not new mathematics: commons overshoot, the proxy problem and lock-in are restated in one small vocabulary, each law machine-checked in Lean from premises it names and set beside its closest prior result. Whether actual markets, judges and trained systems meet those premises is the open part: 33 tests fixed in advance have run, most came out mixed or against, each failure is kept beside its claim, and the work, written with AI under one person's direction, has not yet had independent review.

WHAT NEIGHBOURING WORKS DO ON THEIR FIRST SCREEN THAT THIS DOES NOT:
- Olah and others, "Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits" (Distill, 2020): named authors, affiliation and date; then three claims, numbered, and called speculative by the authors themselves, each with a figure. The uncertainty is said once, as part of the claim, and the reader knows in thirty seconds what would have to be true.
- A Stanford Encyclopedia entry (for instance Seibt, "Process Philosophy"): one neutral paragraph that defines the subject and stands alone, a numbered contents list, the author's name, first-published and revised dates, a bibliography. No statement about itself. This is also what Wikipedia's lead section does, and is the part of "more like a Wikipedia" worth copying.
- ARC, "Eliciting Latent Knowledge" (2021): one problem, one running example (the vault and the diamond) used all the way through, and on the first page the plain statement that the authors have no solution, followed by proposals and the counterexamples that broke them. Failed attempts are the content, told as moves in an argument, not tallied.
- A Lean blueprint page (the Liquid Tensor Experiment, or the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa project): one dependency graph in which every node is a statement in a sentence of prose, coloured by whether it is stated or proved, each linked to its Lean. That is topology a reader can walk, and it is the nearest existing model for the map Ren asked for.
- Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell, "Consequences of Misaligned AI" (NeurIPS 2020), the direct neighbour: the abstract gives one model and one result in two sentences. The account restates their Theorem 1 and says so on the one page two thirds of the way down; a safety researcher should meet that sentence first.
where_ren_may_be_wrong_or_incomplete:
1. "Don't mention AI so much" is right about frequency and wrong if it becomes concealment. The git log shows about 7,000 commits and 294,000 lines of Lean in nine weeks; a visitor who finds that after a front that plays it down will trust nothing. Say it once, prominently, as method, and then stop.
2. No name on the fronts costs more confidence than any hedge. Every work that earns trust quickly has an accountable author on its first line. The repository URL already carries the name.
3. The plain sentence in AGENTS.md is plain but not sized for a sceptic: "how anything forms, persists, changes and ends" is the single largest confidence cost on the first screen, and it is Ren's own sentence. Plainness and credibility are different things; the alignment half (what a selection reaches, drains, locks on) is both plain and credible and should lead.
4. The opening's voice ("Truth exists", "the truth, the dharma, the Dao", "the most important matter ... in the whole history of the Earth") is his and should not be edited, but placed inside the README it is what makes the project read as not serious. Position, not wording, is the fix.
5. "More like a Wikipedia" will not help by itself. The repository already has 563 linked record pages and a search box; what it lacks is Wikipedia's lead section and its human-scale articles. More structure over the same generated mass reproduces the problem. The Stacks Project or a Lean blueprint is the better model.
6. Cutting words naively would cut the distinctions (proved in a model, tested, argued) that are the work's real claim to seriousness, and the failures kept on record, which are its most persuasive content. The fix is order and number of labels, not silence about limits.
7. A topology picture will not earn confidence unless its nodes are things an outsider recognises (overshoot, proxy, lock, renewal) and are chosen by hand. The house rule that pictures are "drawn from the entries alone" and "none typed" guarantees inventories. A map needs an editor.
8. The 4 is a judgment of the face. Underneath, the prior-art table, the review dossiers' questions to specialists (B-02 especially) and the kept counterexamples are better than a 4; a rebuild should surface them, not start over.
9. On dualism I can only say what a philosopher would see from this lens: "no good and evil set over it" is asserted as a slogan and then hedged, while the page still runs on pairs (opens and closes, widens and narrows, reads and lies beyond). The position has serious neighbours (Zhuangzi's 齐物论, Spinoza, Whitehead, constructivism after Korsgaard); arguing it beside them would read as serious where repeating it does not.
